claims.claim: Human resource (HR) management is the process of hiring, developing, motivating, and evaluating employees to achieve organizational goals; OpenStax's Introduction to Business states this working definition, and this lesson attributes it to OpenStax.

The HR management process is sequential: job analysis and design and HR planning come first, then employee recruitment, then employee selection, then training and development, then performance planning and evaluation, then compensation and benefits; the lesson summarizes this sequence in six named stages (recruit, hire, train, evaluate, compensate, offboard) as its own simplified teaching framing.
A job description lists the tasks and responsibilities of a job, while a job specification lists the skills, knowledge, and abilities a person must have to fill it.

Recruitment is the process of attracting qualified people to form an applicant pool; employers draw on the internal labor market (current employees, via promotions and transfers) and the external labor market (applicants outside the firm).

Selection is the process of determining which applicants possess the qualifications necessary to succeed on the job; it commonly runs as successive hurdles including initial screening, employment testing, a selection interview (the tool most widely used in hiring decisions), and background and reference checks.

Organizations invest in training and development so that employees have the knowledge and skills to perform their jobs successfully; training and development involves learning situations in which the employee acquires additional knowledge or skills to increase job performance, delivered on the job through orientation, coaching, job rotation, apprenticeship, and mentoring.

Development serves growth beyond the current job: job rotation and career-mobility programs prepare employees for future roles, and succession planning identifies current employees who can fill vacancies and be promoted.

A performance appraisal is a comparison of actual performance with expected performance, used to determine an employee's contributions and to make decisions about training, compensation, promotion, and other job changes.

Compensation includes both pay and benefits: direct pay is wages or salaries (including base pay), incentive pay includes commissions, bonuses, and profit-sharing, and indirect pay consists of benefits such as health insurance, retirement plans, and vacation time; employers also compare their pay against competitor and market rates because a firm paying far below the market may struggle to attract and keep skilled people.

HR exists because people matter to results: HR practices exist to achieve organizational goals and are described by OpenStax as making employees a key element for gaining competitive advantage, with good HR practices fostering performance improvement, knowledge and skill development, and loyal employees who stay.

Employees eventually leave organizations — they resign, retire, or are let go — and HR manages the transition (exit interviews, final paperwork); post-employment arrangements that employers administer, such as unemployment compensation, show that departure is a normal, managed stage of employment. The lesson names this stage 'offboard', which is this lesson's framing: OpenStax's first-edition process sequence ends at compensation and benefits.

Hiring, managing, and paying employees is a core part of running a business; the U.S. Small Business Administration's Business Guide treats 'Hire and manage employees' as a standard business-management task (U.S. context, described generally in the lesson with no employment-law specifics).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether HR's role is primarily administrative or strategic
positions: Some portrayals treat HR as a paperwork and compliance office that processes hires, pay, and forms.
OpenStax frames HR practices as a decision-support system intended to make employees a key element for gaining competitive advantage, tying every people decision to organizational goals.

The lesson takes the strategic view: HR is a business function that exists because people do the work that produces results, while acknowledging its administrative tasks (job postings, paperwork, transitions).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents HR as a business function tied to organizational goals, per OpenStax, and uses the employee lifecycle to show the administrative and strategic work together.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the employee lifecycle includes an offboarding stage
positions: OpenStax's first-edition HRM process sequence ends at compensation and benefits.
Practitioner framings commonly add separation or offboarding as a final stage, and employers administer post-employment arrangements such as unemployment compensation.
The lesson names six steps including offboard as a simplified teaching framing, grounded in OpenStax's sequence for the other five stages.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the six-step lifecycle (recruit, hire, train, evaluate, compensate, offboard) as its own framing and notes that OpenStax's sequence covers the first five; offboarding is described generally (resign, retire, or be let go, with HR managing the transition).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether training and development are the same activity
positions: The terms are often used interchangeably for any workplace learning.

OpenStax treats training and development as one combined activity (employees acquire knowledge or skills to increase job performance) while its examples distinguish current-job training (orientation, coaching) from future-role preparation (job rotation, career mobility).
The lesson presents two purposes of one investment: skills for the current job and growth beyond it.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches training and development as one activity with two named purposes, matching OpenStax's combined treatment and its examples.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, Section 8.1: Achieving High Performance through Human Resources Management
sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (open textbook). The canonical openstax.org page requires JavaScript, so the section was verified via an Internet Archive capture (2020-09-20) of this canonical URL. Supports: the working definition of HR management as the process of hiring, developing, motivating, and evaluating employees to achieve organizational goals; the sequential HRM process (job analysis and design, planning and forecasting, recruitment, selection, training and development, performance planning and evaluation, compensation and benefits); job description vs job specification; HR practices as the system that makes employees a key element for gaining competitive advantage; succession planning.

sourceRecords.notes: Tier A (U.S. government guidance; U.S. context). Verified live via HTTP on 2026-08-21.
